==Problem==

In how many ways can <imath>345</imath> be written as the sum of an increasing sequence of two or more consecutive positive integers?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ 1\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 3\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 5\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 6\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 7</imath>

==Solution 1==
Factor <imath>345=3\cdot 5\cdot 23</imath>.

Suppose we take an odd number <imath>k</imath> of consecutive integers, with the median as <imath>m</imath>. Then <imath>mk=345</imath> with <imath>\tfrac12k<m</imath>.
Looking at the factors of <imath>345</imath>, the possible values of <imath>k</imath> are <imath>3,5,15,23</imath> with medians as <imath>115,69,23,15</imath> respectively.

Suppose instead we take an even number <imath>2k</imath> of consecutive integers, with median being the average of <imath>m</imath> and <imath>m+1</imath>. Then <imath>k(2m+1)=345</imath> with <imath>k\le m</imath>.
Looking again at the factors of <imath>345</imath>, the possible values of <imath>k</imath> are <imath>1,3,5</imath> with medians <imath>(172,173),(57,58),(34,35)</imath> respectively.

Thus the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) }7}</imath>.

==Solution 2==

We need to find consecutive numbers (an arithmetic sequence that increases by <imath>1</imath>) that sums to <imath>345</imath>. This calls for the sum of an arithmetic sequence given that the first term is <imath>k</imath>, the last term is <imath>g</imath> and with <imath>n</imath> elements, which is: <imath>\frac {n \cdot (k+g)}{2}</imath>.

We look for sequences of <imath>n</imath> consecutive numbers starting at <imath>k</imath> and ending at <imath>k+n-1</imath>. We can now substitute <imath>g</imath> with <imath>k+n-1</imath>. Now we substitute our new value of <imath>g</imath> into <imath>\frac {n \cdot (k+g)}{2}</imath> to get that the sum is <imath>\frac {n \cdot (k+k+n-1)}{2} = 345</imath>.

This simplifies to <imath>\frac {n \cdot (2k+n-1)}{2} = 345</imath>. This gives a nice equation. We multiply out the 2 to get that <imath>n \cdot (2k+n-1)=690</imath>. This leaves us with 2 integers that multiply to <imath>690</imath> which leads us to think of factors of <imath>690</imath>. We know the factors of <imath>690</imath> are:  <imath>1,2,3,5,6,10,15,23,30,46,69,115,138,230,345,690</imath>. So through inspection (checking), we see that only <imath>2,3,5,6,10,15</imath> and <imath>23</imath> work. This gives us the answer of <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) }7}</imath> ways.

An alternate way to start.

Let the sequence have \(k\) terms starting from a positive integer \(a\). The sum of this sequence is given by the arithmetic series formula:\(S=\frac{k}{2}[2a+(k-1)]\)We are given \(S = 345\), with the constraints \(k \geq 2\) and \(a \geq 1\). Multiplying both sides by \(2\) gives:\(2\times 345=k(2a+k-1)\)\(690=k(2a+k-1)\)

An alternate way to finish.

Let 
<cmath>
\begin{align*}
2k+n-1 &=\frac{690}{k} \\
n &= k \\
\end{align*}
</cmath>
where <imath>k</imath> is a factor of <imath>690.</imath>
We find <imath>2k = 1+\frac{690}{k}-k</imath> so we need <imath>\frac{690}{k} - k</imath> to be positive and odd. Fortunately, regardless of the parity of <imath>k</imath> we see that <imath>\frac{690}{k} - k</imath> is odd. Furthermore, we need <imath>\frac{690}{k} >k</imath> which eliminates exact half of the factors. Now, since we need more than <imath>1</imath> integer to sum up we need <imath>k \ge 2</imath> which eliminates one more case. There were <imath>16</imath> cases to begin with, so our answer is <imath>\frac{16}{2}-1 = \boxed{\textbf{(E) }7}</imath> ways.

==Solution 2.1==
At the very end of Solution 2, where we find the factors of 690, instead of inspection, notice that all numbers will work until you get to <imath>30</imath>, and that is because <imath>\frac{345}{30}=11.5</imath>, which means <imath>11</imath> and <imath>12</imath> must be the middle 2 numbers; however, a sequence of length <imath>30</imath> with middle numbers <imath>11</imath> and <imath>12</imath> that consists only of integers would go into the negatives, so any number from 30 onwards wouldn't work, and since <imath>1</imath> is a trivial, non-counted solution, we get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) }7}</imath> -ColtsFan10

==Solution 3 (Fast And Clean)==
The median of the sequence <imath>m</imath> is either an integer or a half integer. Let <imath>m=\frac{i}{2}, i \in N</imath>, then <imath>P=i\cdot n=2\cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 23</imath>. 

On the other hand we have two constraints: 

1) <imath>m \geq \frac{n+1}{2} \iff i>n</imath> because the integers in the sequence are all positive, and <imath>n>1</imath>;

2) If <imath>n</imath> is odd then <imath>m</imath> is an integer, <imath>i</imath> is even; if <imath>n</imath> is even then <imath>m</imath> is a half integer, <imath>i</imath> is odd. Therefore, <imath>n</imath> and <imath>i</imath> have opposite parity.

Now <imath>P</imath> has <imath>16</imath> factors and it is not a perfect square. There are <imath>8-1=7</imath> choices for <imath>1 < n < \sqrt{P}</imath>. Also since <imath>2|P, 4\nmid P</imath>, we know <imath>n</imath> and <imath>\frac{P}{n}</imath> must have opposite parity. Therefore the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) }7}</imath>.

==Solution 4==
You can find consecutive ways by checking individual numbers. For example, if you want <imath>2</imath> consecutive numbers to add to <imath>345</imath>, you can set up 
<cmath>\begin{split}
a+(a+1) &=345 \\
2a+1 &=345 \\
2a &= 344 \\
a &= 172
\end{split}</cmath>
<imath>172+173=345</imath>. For <imath>4</imath> you would do <imath>(a-1)+a+(a+1)+(a+2)</imath> or <imath>4a+2</imath>. For <imath>6</imath> it would be <imath>6a+3</imath>, so for any even number it would be in the form <imath>ka+\frac{k}{2}</imath>. For all multiples of <imath>4</imath> you can rule out since they are dividing by an even number after taking away an even number, and 345 is odd so it would not turn out to be a whole number.

For odd numbers it will center around the middle. Take <imath>3</imath> as an example:
<cmath>\begin{split}
(a-1)+a+(a+1) &=345 \\
3a &=345 \\
a &= 115
\end{split}</cmath>
<imath>114+115+116=345</imath>. You can see that for odd numbers that if you put <imath>a</imath> in the middle all the numbers will cancel out and become the center number. For <imath>5</imath> it would just be <imath>5a</imath>. For all odd numbers it will just be <imath>ka</imath>. 

Using this method and testing you will find that <imath>2,3,5,6,20,15</imath> and <imath>23</imath> work. At <imath>23</imath> you will notice that the center is <imath>15</imath>, and that the first number is <imath>4</imath>, so by intuition you are done. On top of that, <imath>7</imath> is the highest possible answer so with certainty you can say that you're answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E)}7}</imath>.
